prize_parts.citation: For an oeuvre of poetry, verse novel and essay that renews the book-length form through a sustained dialogue with antiquity, joining formal invention to elegiac and erotic intensity.

statement.case_for: After the exchange my laureate is unchanged, but I hold it more narrowly. On public knowledge, Carson's voice is distinctive. Autobiography of Red turns a fragmentary Greek source into a modern verse novel about desire and selfhood. Nox builds an elegy as an object whose form is part of the mourning. Her essays on Greek eros and ancient texts belong to the same practice of making an inherited form carry present feeling. In these works the formal invention is not ornament; it is how the work thinks about loss and desire. That meets the common criteria of voice, formal and linguistic achievement, imaginative and intellectual depth, and significance across a body of work. I can read her in the original language, so one uncertainty is lower than for most shortlisted candidates. That lowers a risk and is not merit. In answer to the chair's question about the credited core: Autobiography of Red, Nox and the essays, with the verse and prose collections around them. The classical versions are context and not part of the credited achievement. I accept a citation limited to original poetry, verse novel and essays. The citation above is worded that way, and it does not make the book-as-object the main claim, because I cannot judge that dimension from description. This is a judgment from public knowledge and not a fresh reading or independent verification of the corpus.
statement.case_against: Round 1 left real weaknesses in my own case and I do not think the exchange removed them. First, the demonstrable weight sits on a handful of titles, and I cannot say that the later and more performance-oriented books sustain the level of Autobiography of Red and Nox. Carlberg asked for a colleague with closer knowledge to test this, and I support that request, since I cannot do it from the supplied evidence. Second, the hybrid format may prove influential mainly among writers and not canonical. Third, Cărtărescu's single, statable project at very large scale is a stronger answer to 'whole oeuvre' than Carson's range, and Olsson and Mattson are right that this is the main rival consideration. If the committee reads the will's 'ideal direction' as favoring visionary scale, my preference could reasonably be overturned. Michon's compression is rigorous, but the small corpus counts against a whole-oeuvre citation, so I keep him as an alternative and not my first choice.

responses.point: Olsson prefers Cărtărescu because his project has a more stable centre. He says the open questions about him concern reading quality (translation, excess), while those about Carson concern delimiting the corpus. He also asks the committee to argue the merits of each oeuvre directly, without leaning on opening counts.
responses.response: I accept the distinction, and I think it is accurate. The delimiting problem is real, and I have answered it by narrowing the citation to the original poetry, verse novel and essays. That narrowing has a cost: it honours a smaller corpus than the word 'oeuvre' suggests. I would add that the open questions about Cărtărescu are not lighter. Neither of us can read the Romanian prose directly, so excess or repetition in the long novels cannot be tested by us, and the early poetry is the least accessible part. A question about reading quality that cannot be answered is not better for the case than a boundary that can be drawn. On the will's wording, I now read 'ideal direction' as seriousness of purpose and depth, not scale. On that reading both candidates qualify, and the choice goes back to weighting. I still weigh range of formal reinvention, and my ability to judge it in the original, slightly above sustained scale. I hold that weighting with real uncertainty and I would not treat it as decisive if close reading of the later Cărtărescu novels showed that they deepen the project.

responses.point: Mattson argues that Cărtărescu's project can be stated in one sentence and sustained across decades, while Carson's range across scholarship, lyric, essay and object-book makes a single defining achievement harder to name. She says this is about how clearly the oeuvre coheres, not about which invention is greater.
responses.response: That is the strongest form of the objection and I want to answer it without waving it away. My attempt at one sentence: Carson makes inherited forms carry present grief and desire by reshaping the form itself, in verse novel, elegy and essay. That is a method, and I recognise it is less compact than a single metaphysical architecture. Coherence of method is not the same as coherence of a world, and I concede that the second is easier to cite. I do not think it follows that the first is the lesser achievement. I also accept your correction of the readership point. In round 1 I treated the narrowing of readership through allusiveness as a possible weakness. After the exchange I withdraw it as a criterion. I keep only the narrower concern that the case rests on a limited number of titles. Your warning about excess in the large novels is the same kind of concern, and it cuts against both of us equally.

responses.point: Palm asks whether the hybrid formats will last in the canon or remain influential mainly among peers. She suggests the lyric and narrative strengths appear within the hybrid forms and that the emotional matter of Nox is available without specialist knowledge. She also states her weighting for formal economy and compressed lyric invention explicitly.
responses.response: I agree with her on the main point: the hybrid form is where the lyric and narrative strengths are located, so I would not set the hybrid books against a more conventional body of work. The question of durability I still cannot answer, and I would not claim to. What I can say is that the emotional force of Autobiography of Red and Nox gives them a claim beyond specialist circles, and that this is a judgment from public knowledge and not a verified account of reception. Her explicit weighting helps me compare the two cases, because mine is similar. Where I would be more cautious than she is: formal economy is a strength of Nox, but it is harder to claim across the whole corpus, so the citation should not promise it.

responses.point: Sward suggests anchoring the citation in the written text, treating Nox's physical form as an extension and not a substitute. She also says the choice between Carson and Cărtărescu turns on how much weight goes to unity of project against breadth of formal reinvention, and she cannot fully resolve it.
responses.response: I adopt her anchoring. It keeps the citation inside what the committee can assess from the printed work, and it avoids claiming a dimension that none of us can judge from description. I also share her statement that the weighting cannot be fully resolved by argument. The most I can do is say what would move me: a close account of the later Cărtărescu novels showing that they extend the project, and a close account of Carson's later books showing that they do not merely repeat the earlier devices. Neither is available in the supplied evidence, so the vote I cast will rest on public knowledge and I will say so.

uncertainties: My assessment rests on public knowledge of the major works and the supplied longlist summaries, not on a fresh reading or independent verification of the corpus.
Whether Carson's later and more performance-oriented books sustain the level of Autobiography of Red and Nox cannot be settled from the evidence I have.
Whether the hybrid books will be canonical or remain influential mainly among writers is open.
A text-only reading understates Nox and similar works, and the citation must not claim more than the written text supports.
For Cărtărescu, I cannot assess the sentence-level patterning of the Romanian or whether the long novels lapse into excess. Coverage of his early poetry in translation is also uncertain.
For Michon, the small corpus and the translatability of compressed French prose limit a whole-oeuvre judgment.
The committee has not agreed a common reading of the will's 'ideal direction'. My own reading as seriousness of purpose is one interpretation among several.
Carlberg is co-opted and her voting status is undocumented. How much weight a four-vote majority should place on her simulated vote is a modeling assumption and not a literary question.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile, which records no personal, institutional or collaborative tie to any shortlisted writer. Two limits should be disclosed. My profile notes that my work as a critic at Dagens Nyheter was not surveyed, so I cannot rule out earlier reviews of a shortlisted writer. My own practice as a novelist of documentary historical fiction is context only and is not evidence of a preference for any candidate. The 2025 laureate remarks attributed to me do not establish a voting preference.
